title: UGC 9391
caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 9391, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 9391 · constellation Draco · about 130 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy UGC 9391, which lies about 130 million light-years away in the constellation of Draco. The galaxy played a part in measuring how fast the Universe is expanding today.

Inside UGC 9391 are Cepheid variable stars. These stars brighten and fade in a regular rhythm, and the length of that rhythm is linked to how bright they truly are. By comparing that true brightness with how bright they appear, astronomers can work out their distance.

The galaxy also hosted a Type Ia supernova, a kind of stellar explosion whose brightness can likewise be used to judge distance, though it is not visible here. A team of astronomers used both the Cepheids and the supernova in this galaxy as part of their calculation of the expansion rate of the modern Universe, making it one step on a longer ladder of distance measurements.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.85 x 1.85 arcminutes) and distance (130 million light years), the frame spans roughly 70,000 × 70,000 light-years. Its light set out about 130 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters at 350, 555 and 814 nm, from near-ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Some of this light lies outside the range the eye can see, and Hubble's exposures reveal a galaxy far too faint to view in any detail by eye.
